#13 Summary conclusion

ID Logistics offers a positively skewed 18-month case: the revenue step-up is already reported, the earnings step-up follows by arithmetic in 2027 to 2028, and the shares trade below their median multiple while estimates rise.

ID Logistics is a disciplined, founder-run replicator of a thin-margin but very sticky contract-logistics model. The company has just put through the largest two-year launch cohort in its history, because e-commerce customers pulled it into North America and Australia. The cohort's revenue is already in the reported numbers. The cohort's earnings follow as its contracts pass breakeven in 2027 to 2028. The shares were de-rated in early 2026 for a cash miss that the H1 2026 results reversed, and they now sit below their median multiple while estimates rise.

The case is a Demand-driven EPSU with a positive skew. The case's single real test is whether the underlying EBIT margin and year-end cash hold through the two results releases of March and August 2027.

The two dates that decide the case: FY2026 results in mid-March 2027 (underlying EBIT margin of 4.45% or more, working capital under 4% of sales) and H1 2027 results in late August 2027 (margin up 20bp or more).

#0 The investment case: customers are pulling ID Logistics into new countries, revenue has stepped up, and the margin should follow in 2027

The one idea: ID Logistics' reported margin is a weighted average of a profitable back book of mature contracts and a loss-making front book of new ones, so earnings swing with the mix between the two.

ID Logistics runs dedicated, single-client warehouses for retailers, e-commerce platforms and consumer-goods brands in 20 countries. The company owns no property and matches every lease and forklift contract to the five-to-six-year customer contract behind it. Customers pay per pallet and parcel handled, with annual inflation indexation, so revenue follows the clients' physical volumes rather than their prices or profits. Every new contract loses money for its first 12 to 18 months and then earns a 20 to 25% post-tax return on capital, rising to 40% on renewal.

Three consequences follow. The competitive position rests on execution and on renewal rates above 90%. The main risk is that the front book grows faster than the back book can carry it. Earnings are highly sensitive to the mix, because a 4.4% EBIT margin sits on top of about EUR 80m of lease and financial interest: each 10bp of margin is worth about 3.5% of earnings per share.

The change: the front book is growing at a record pace, and for the right reason, because customers are pulling ID Logistics into new countries. Like-for-like growth accelerated from 16% in 2025 to 17% in Q1, 23% in Q2 and 25% in Q3 2026. North America grew 48% organically in Q3 on e-commerce launches in the US and Canada. Australia opened in H1 2026 as the 20th country, to follow an existing e-commerce client, and Germany's network has doubled to 17 sites since 2021. ID Logistics launched 27 contracts in 2025 against 20 guided, and plans 25 to 27 in 2026, with the upper end flagged.

The forces behind the launch wave are secular and uncontroversial. Outsourcing penetration is still only 15% in North America and 25% in Europe. E-commerce is 25% of group sales, and its 30% return rates need labour-heavy sorting. Retailers want multi-country partners who can automate, and 80% of ID Logistics' proposals now carry a robotics solution. The headwinds are real but modest: France (26% of sales) grows at mid-single digits under a 150bp sovereign premium, labour inflation runs ahead of each contract's annual indexation date, and the euro-reporting group hedges none of its 30% non-euro revenue.

How the change reaches the financials: revenue leads in 2026, the margin follows in 2027, and a slow-growing interest line turns both into faster EPS growth. In 2026 the record launch cohort lifts revenue by about 20% while launch losses hold the EBIT margin near 4.4 to 4.5%, so EBIT grows about 20%. Because interest grows more slowly than EBIT, EPS grows about 28%, to about EUR 12.5 from EUR 9.73 (brokers' adjusted basis) in 2025. In 2027 the 2025 and 2026 cohorts pass breakeven while the launch count normalises, so revenue growth slows to about 12% but the margin steps up 20bp to about 4.65%, and EPS grows about 24%. The setup: the case fits Richard's "Demand-driven EPSU" best. Demand (outsourcing, e-commerce, and following customers into North America and Australia) is stepping the revenue base up by a fifth, and the J-curve converts that higher revenue into a step-up in earnings power in 2027 to 2028.

Present in the setup

  • A visible, accelerating demand signal.
  • Conservative guidance: 11 to 13% organic growth framed against 22% delivered.
  • Sell-side upgrades already running.
  • A two-year-forward multiple at the 42nd percentile of its ten-year range and the 29th of five years, after a de-rating from 28x to 20x on FY2025 cash-conversion worries that the H1 2026 results have since reversed.

Missing from the setup

  • The margin inflection is not yet in the numbers: the H1 2026 underlying EBIT margin rose 20bp, within noise.
  • Technical momentum is rated D, with the price flat over twelve months.
  • The thin free float and six-broker coverage make the narrative slow to spread.

A secondary "CfC clearing" element is also present: the FY2025 working-capital drain cleared in H1 2026, and French political risk is the residual CfC. The EPSU, not the CfC clearing, carries the return.

The reward and the skew: the skew is positive because the revenue leg is already delivered and the multiple is below its median, so the case needs the margin leg only to hold, not to surprise. If the case plays out, two-year-forward EPS rolls from about EUR 17.9 today to about EUR 20 to 21 by end-2027 to mid-2028 (+12 to 17%), and the multiple reverts from 21.4x towards the guideline 28.6x (+34%). The result is a return of about +50 to +56% over 13 to 18 months, with no dividend; at the Analyst's own fairer 25x the return is about +34%. If the case fails, with the margin stalled at 4.4% and growth slowing to 8%, EPS falls about 10% against consensus and the multiple revisits its 2026 low near 18x, for a loss of about 20%. Weighting the base case at 50%, the better case at 25% and the worse case at 25% gives about +27% over 18 months.

What has to be true: three releases must confirm growth, then margin and cash, then the margin step.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment: a clear net tailwind for revenue, a mild headwind for margin

The operating environment lifts the revenue line and only trims the margin line, which is exactly the shape of the investment case.

Contract logistics grows at 4 to 6% a year, about 200bp above GDP, driven by outsourcing and e-commerce. Demand is volume-based and defensive: the sector has grown through recessions because it is paid per unit handled, not per euro sold, and renewal rates run at 90 to 95% across the industry. Supply conditions help on balance. French logistics vacancy has risen to 7%, which caps rent inflation for a tenant that leases all its sites, while modern automated big-box space remains scarce, which protects operators with existing networks.

The environment lifts the revenue line and only trims the margin line.

The Fitness-for-Fighting digest reads the European regime as risk-off beneath an index high, with the consumer weak, and the Geography digest flags France as a double-underweight country. The ID Logistics case does not need a lower discount rate to work, because it compounds on volumes, but it does carry a French label that the market is currently penalising.

Consensus and the Analyst agree on the demand picture. The Analyst is more positive on France: the French drag is already small in the mix (24% of H1 2026 revenue) and shrinks by two points a year.

Counter-case: a European consumer recession would cut volumes at fixed-cost dedicated sites, and the claim that volume-based contracts insulate the business has not been tested in a genuine downturn since 2009. Two signals would change the Analyst's view: French like-for-like growth turning negative for two quarters, or client tender activity rising above the 20 to 25% of revenue that renews each year.

Conclusion: the operating environment supports double-digit volume growth and offers no headwind large enough to stop it. The environment supports step 2 of the case (the change is externally driven and durable) and leaves open only the margin cost of labour inflation.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. Structural, volume-based external demand (outsourcing only 15% penetrated in North America and 25% in Europe, e-commerce 25% of sales with labour-heavy returns, customers pulling the company into the US, Canada and Australia) adds clearly to organic growth, though the market itself grows only 4-6% and much of the 20%-plus is share gain; France (24-26% of sales, mature, sovereign premium), labour inflation ahead of indexation and unhedged FX trim the margin side. Consensus sales growth at the 83rd percentile is honest but partly company-driven, so a clear net positive below a funded, order-book-backed force: between Eckert & Ziegler (72) and Linea Directa (63).

#2 Internally driven change forces: steady and supportive, but incremental rather than transformational

The internal change is incremental rather than transformational. None of the internal programmes is a restructuring or a new business model; together they apply the same follow-the-customer, asset-light replication harder and with more technology. That incrementalism is a strength for predictability and a limit for upside: the margin step-up depends on cohort maturation and productivity, not on a cost programme with a quantified target.

Problems and risks: voluntary staff turnover rose to 15.1% in 2024 from 12.3%, a real cost in a people business. A USD 2.36m False Claims Act settlement at the acquired Kane Logistics (August 2026) shows gaps in acquisition compliance. The deputy CEO halved his stake in 2025, the executive succession plan was formalised only in 2025, and the only substantive board committee is a two-person audit committee.

Market view against the Analyst's: the sell-side credits the technology programme with a 10bp annual margin gain; the Analyst thinks that is about right and would not underwrite more. The Analyst differs on the weight of M&A. Consensus models no acquisitions, and the Analyst also models none, but the probability of a North American bolt-on acquisition within 18 months is meaningful, and such a deal would broaden the thesis narrative more than it would add to EPS.

Conclusion: internal forces are steady and supportive, not a source of surprise. They support step 4 of the case (the foundation is a proven replication machine) and leave the margin leg of step 3 reliant on cohort maturation rather than on a programme Richard can track.

I weigh this higher than the memo's 'incremental': entering Australia as the 20th country, the North American build-out (48% organic in Q3), Canada, a record 27 then 25-27 launches a year and robotics in 80% of proposals are large, funded strategic moves already showing in revenue, with a reopened EUR 400-500m M&A capacity; but the margin payoff is not yet in reported earnings and there are internal drags (turnover up to 15.1%, the Kane compliance settlement, thin board committees, deputy CEO selling). Real and working but outputs lagging: between Theon (71) and OEM International (66).

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management: a sticky, well-run business in the thinnest stage of the value chain

ID Logistics is a medium-to-high-quality business in a thin-margin industry, run by an aligned but unchecked founder; its financial profile is excellent on leverage and growth and ordinary on margin and equity cash flow.

Value chain: contract logistics is the thin stage of a chain in which others take the rents. Property developers (CTP at an 88% adjusted operating margin), warehouse-management-system software vendors (Manhattan at 35%) and consolidated less-than-truckload carriers (Old Dominion at 25%) earn far more than dedicated warehousing, which earns 3 to 6% EBIT.

Industry structure: pricing power is weak at the bid and strong at renewal. The market is extremely fragmented: the leader, DHL, has 6%, and ID Logistics has about 1% globally and 1.1 to 1.2% in Europe, where it ranks sixth. 68% of warehousing is still run in-house, and tenders are formal and open-book. Barriers to entry come from execution, customer-specific IT and mechanisation, and switching costs: renewal rates are above 90%, the average remaining contract term is about four years, and the top three customers are 26% of sales across 66 contracts. Competitors describe ID Logistics as a disciplined but aggressive bidder that prices to win and then recovers price at renewal, which is consistent with both the J-curve and the 20 to 25% contract ROIC.

Financial profile: cash is the weak spot. Revenue has compounded at 15% over three years and 14% a year since 2019, and the underlying EBIT margin has held at 4.2 to 4.6% through the cycle (above GXO's 3.5 to 4%, below DHL Supply Chain's 6% and DSV Solutions' 9%). The EBITDA margin is 15.6% on the brokers' basis, inflated by leases; group ROIC is about 13%; pre-IFRS 16 leverage is 0.6x, with EUR 250m of unused credit lines; and the company has never paid a dividend. Free cash flow to equity after lease cash is thin (the Analyst estimates EUR 20 to 50m a year through 2028), because about 30% of each new contract's annual sales is invested up front and lease liabilities (EUR 1,310m) grow with the footprint. The FY2025 working-capital outflow of EUR 65m showed how fast that cash cost can bite.

Management and culture: an aligned founder with a long delivery record. The founder-owner has run the company for 25 years, invested family money at the start, kept the message consistent, and delivered every five-year revenue target. A long-serving CFO guides prudently. Internal promotion fills 76% of French site-manager posts, and the company holds a top-ten global workplace ranking.

Governance: concentrated and lightly checked. The founders hold 64% of votes for 50% of capital. The company pays the CEO's family holding EUR 1.2m a year under a management agreement, related-party rentals are rising, there is no remuneration committee, the company follows the Middlenext code rather than Afep-Medef, and the deputy CEO sold EUR 29m of stock at about EUR 396 a share.

Market view against the Analyst's: the market treats ID Logistics as a growth compounder with a founder discount. The Analyst agrees, and adds that the market under-weights the renewal economics (40% ROIC on renewal) and over-weights the lease liabilities, which are back-to-back with customer contracts.

Conclusion: the business's quality supports step 4 of the case, and its thin margin and governance are the reasons the fair multiple should sit below the top of the stock's range.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a sticky, execution-led position (renewals above 90%, switching costs from customer-specific IT and mechanisation, 20-25% contract ROIC and 40% on renewal, a founder with a 25-year delivery record) inside a thin, fragmented stage of the value chain where landlords and software vendors take the rents and pricing is weak at the bid; governance is concentrated. The figures (operating margin 14th percentile, reported ROIC 3.6% at the 27th, distorted by leases and goodwill against a 13% group ROIC) understate it, and predictability is high, so above typical but below Helios Towers' structurally stronger unit economics: between Helios Towers (60) and Shell (54).

#4 Guidance conservatism and delivery record: excellent on the top line, silent on margin and cash

ID Logistics structurally under-promises on the top line and lets consensus chase. The pattern helps the case because it makes a beat the most likely outcome at every sales release. The weakness is that the margin and cash lines, where the real test lies, carry no guidance at all, so a disappointment on either would arrive without warning.

Management gives no profit guidance and frames only organic growth and launches. Delivery has beaten the framing in each of the last three years (chart below): FY2024 was framed at about 10% and delivered 17% like-for-like; FY2025 was framed at 9 to 11% and delivered 16%; FY2026 was framed at 9 to 11%, raised to 11 to 13% in July, and is running at about 22% after nine months. Launches also beat (27 in 2025 against 20 guided), and sales beat Bloomberg consensus by 8% in Q2 2026 and 7% in Q3. The H1 2026 underlying EBIT margin rose 20bp to 3.9% while 17 sites launched.

The one miss was cash: FY2025 free cash flow disappointed on receivables, and the shares fell about 20% in March 2026 before H1 2026 collections reversed the shortfall.

The sell-side anchors on management's framing and catches up after each release. All six brokers rate the shares Buy, with a median target of EUR 513. FY2027 consensus EPS has been revised up 9% in six months and 4% in three. Bernstein alone has lifted its target three times since April (EUR 470 to 525), while trimming its reported EPS once (August) for launch costs and interest before raising it again in October. Consensus FY2026 EPS has ranged from EUR 11.5 to 13.3 over the year, and the six brokers' FY2026 estimates are widely dispersed, from EUR 11.5 to 14.5.

Counter-case: the 7 to 8% sales beats partly reflect a consensus that is slow to update rather than genuine conservatism, and Bernstein notes that part of Q3's strength came from indexation pricing and base effects. A quarter in which sales merely meet consensus would change the Analyst's view, because it would signal that the launch wave has peaked.

Conclusion: guidance is deliberately conservative and the top-line delivery record is excellent; the margin and cash record is good but uncovered by guidance. The record supports step 3 of the case (upgrades come through the sales line) and leaves the margin leg to the results in March and August 2027.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. The de facto guide (organic growth framing) has been beaten by 5-9 points three years running (about 10% vs 17%, 9-11% vs 16%, 11-13% raised in July vs about 22%), launches beat (27 vs 20), sales beat consensus 7-8% in the last two quarters and FY2027 EPS is up 9% over six months; the absence of profit guidance is neutral. Held back by the FY2025 cash miss that cost 20% of the price and by margin and cash lines carrying no guide: between Ithaca Energy (80) and Maersk (75).

#5 Operating and financial leverage: three modest gears turn 12% revenue growth into about 24% EPS growth

Revenue growth converts into outsized EPS growth through the J-curve and a heavy fixed interest line, which is why 12% revenue growth can carry 24% EPS growth in 2027. The leverage supports step 3 of the case directly and is the mechanism behind judgement 1 (the 2027 margin step).

  1. Gear 1, operating leverage inside each contract (the J-curve): each contract makes start-up losses for 12 to 18 months, then earns a 20 to 25% post-tax ROIC, and 40% on renewal; 20 to 25% of revenue is re-tendered each year. At group level, the margin therefore rises when launch intensity falls relative to the back book: 27 launches on EUR 3.7bn of revenue in 2025 was 0.7 launches per EUR 100m, 26 launches on EUR 4.5bn in 2026 is 0.6, and 22 on EUR 5.0bn in 2027 would be 0.45.
  2. Gear 2, financial leverage: pre-tax profit is about 60% of EBIT, because EUR 80m-plus of lease and financial interest sits between the two, so EBIT growth of 17% in 2027 becomes pre-tax growth of about 24% if interest grows 8%.
  3. Gear 3, pricing: indexation passes inflation through with a lag of up to a year, and open-book or hybrid contract structures protect the downside while capping the upside.

A fall in the launch cadence to 20 a year would raise the margin faster but cut 2028 growth; management has consistently resolved that trade-off in favour of growth.

Reinforcing loops: new countries follow existing customers (Canada and Australia), so each win lowers the cost of winning the next; mechanisation capex re-invoiced to customers raises switching costs and the odds of renewal; and negative broad working capital funds growth. One loop cuts the other way: growth consumes cash up front, so free cash flow to equity stays thin until growth slows.

Market view against the Analyst's: consensus has EBITDA margins of 15.6 to 15.7% and EBIT margins rising about 15bp a year, close to the Analyst's. The Analyst thinks the market does not price the financial-leverage gear: 28% EPS growth on 20% EBIT growth in 2026 is arithmetic, not optimism, and the same arithmetic repeats in 2027.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Three real but modest gears: J-curve mix leverage as launch intensity falls (0.7 to 0.45 launches per EUR 100m), a fixed EUR 80m-plus interest and lease line that turns 17% EBIT growth into about 24% pre-tax, and follow-the-customer loops; but contracts are largely variable-cost and labour-heavy, pricing is indexation pass-through with open-book caps and no real price power at the bid, and margin moves only 10-20bp a year. Forecast EPS growth of about 20% a year on about 12% revenue is a ratio near 1.6, below the Universe median of about 2, so moderate gearing with no strong single gear, a little above typical for the financial leverage.

#6 Forecast financials: about 20% a year EPS growth, slightly above consensus, with revenue the firm leg and margin the uncertain one

Double-digit revenue growth for four years with a modest margin uplift gives EPS growth of about 20% a year, slightly above consensus. Revenue is the firm leg of the forecast and margin the uncertain one. The forecasts support step 3 of the case and set the base for topics #7 and #12.

The Analyst's forecasts (brokers' basis) are the model's forecasts of record shown in the table below, rounded. The underlying EBIT margin rises from 4.45% in FY2026 (EBIT EUR 199m) to 4.65% in FY2027 (EUR 233m) and 4.8% in FY2028 (EUR 263m). The Analyst's EPS is EUR 12.5, 15.5, 18.1, 20.1 and 22.3 for FY2026 to FY2030. Against consensus EPS of EUR 12.43, 14.77, 17.48 and 19.75 for FY2026 to FY2029, the Analyst is level in 2026 and 3 to 5% ahead in 2027 to 2028.

Phasing and cash assumptions: H2 2026 growth of 21% at a 15.9% EBITDA margin; H1 2027 growth of 13% at 15.2%; H2 2027 growth of 11% at 16.1%. Capex runs at EUR 210 to 225m a year, falling from 4.7% of sales to 3.5%; working capital is 3.5% of sales at each year-end; lease principal is about 8% of sales; and there are no acquisitions and no dividend.

Scope for higher growth and margins than in the past: revenue growth of 20% in 2026 would be the highest organic rate in the company's listed history, and 12% in 2027 would still be above the five-year average once the 2022 Kane acquisition is excluded from the 14% headline average. An underlying EBIT margin of 4.8% by 2028 would be a record, above the 4.6% of 2023, but below management's 5.0 to 5.5% long-run range. On the Analyst's numbers EPS compounds at about 23% a year from 2025 to 2028, against 22% on consensus. Free cash flow to equity after leases stays thin (EUR 23 to 52m a year through 2028), which the market should expect and sometimes forgets.

Counter-case: Bernstein's own reported-EPS trim in August 2026, for launch costs and interest, is the template for how the Analyst's 2027 EPS could be wrong by 5 to 8%. An H2 2026 underlying EBIT margin below 4.8% would change the Analyst's view, because it would put FY2026 at about 4.35%, down year on year.

#7 Scope for upgrades: moderate on revenue, binary on margin and cash

Scope for upgrades over 6 to 12 months is moderate on the revenue line (3 to 5% on 2027 to 2028 EPS) and binary on the margin and cash lines, which puts the weight on two dates: March and August 2027.

What consensus already holds: FY2026 revenue of EUR 4,480m (+20%), then +11% in FY2027 and +9% in FY2028; EBIT margins of 4.45%, 4.6% and 4.75%; and EPS of EUR 12.43, 14.77 and 17.48. The sell-side has already moved: FY2027 EPS +9% and sales +8% over six months, and targets +6%. Those past revisions are momentum (topic #8), not remaining scope.

What consensus does not yet hold: three sources support the Analyst's 2027 revenue 1% above consensus and EPS 5% above.

  1. The annualisation of the 2026 cohort. About ten launches in H2 2026 contribute a full year only in 2027. With an exit run-rate of 17 to 25% like-for-like, consensus growth of 11% for 2027 looks like the same anchoring on management's 8 to 10% framing that produced the 2025 and 2026 beats.
  2. The FX turn. Strategists at Morgan Stanley and Deutsche Bank see EUR/USD at 1.08 in H1 2027, a 1 to 1.5% tailwind to euro revenue and EPS on an unhedged 30% non-euro revenue base.
  3. The wide dispersion among the six brokers (FY2026 EPS EUR 11.5 to 14.5), which means the median moves as the laggards update after each release.

The Analyst cannot name evidence on the margin that the sell-side lacks, so the Analyst's margin assumption sits at consensus.

Market view against the Analyst's: the market expects steady upward drift in estimates, and so does the Analyst, with the March 2027 cash print as the one event that could break the pattern in either direction.

Score: 67, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely raised again in mid-2027 because the 8-10% framing for 2027 ignores the annualising 2026 cohort and a 17-25% exit rate; consensus EPS looks about 5% low for 2027-2028 (about 0.4 times revenue growth, roughly the 60th percentile), with FX a small extra, and the narrative has the most room (six small brokers, no North American deal yet). The margin and cash lines are binary at the March 2027 print, so scope is good rather than strong: between AT&S (71) and Munters (66).

The twelve-month shape (EPS +3%, price (1)%, multiple from 27x to 22x) says the de-rating was about cash conversion and France, not about earnings, and the H1 2026 results answered the cash-conversion concern.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the case: simple to track, moderate earnings risk, lumpy price risk

The case is simple and its earnings risk moderate, but its price risk is lumpy around two cash prints a year and a French label. The risk profile qualifies step 6 of the case: the skew is positive, but the worse case is a fast 20% fall, not a slow drift.

Simplicity: the case has two drivers, like-for-like growth and the underlying EBIT margin, both reported semi-annually with quarterly sales in between, and one cash line (working capital at year-end). Revenue is the most trackable line in European mid-caps, because contracts are signed six months ahead and renewals run at 90%-plus.

Cash prints move the price suddenly; earnings risks arrive gradually and visibly.

Suddenness and materiality: the risks that move the price suddenly are cash prints and macro labels; earnings risk is gradual and visible. Contract logistics has had no demand-led earnings collapse in the listed era. Its failures have been integration-led (DSV's road business in 2026, GXO's site losses in 2025) or cash-led (ID Logistics in 2025). Cyclicality of the business is low (volume-based, dedicated, indexed), but the stock's multiple is cyclical: it fell from 38.8x in December 2021 to 19.1x in September 2022.

Prevalence: the risks are mostly idiosyncratic and trackable, not sector-wide. The environment digest's double-underweight on France and its fragility reading apply to ID Logistics, but the case answers fragility with 0.6x leverage and EUR 250m of undrawn credit lines rather than needing the market to rise.

Market view against the Analyst's: the Risks report rates the bear case at medium probability. The Analyst rates the earnings bear case low-to-medium and the multiple bear case medium, because the stock has shown that it de-rates on cash before it de-rates on profit.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. The case is simple and trackable (two drivers, like-for-like growth and underlying margin, with revenue contracted six months ahead and renewals above 90%) and cyclicality is low; next-year EPS is within roughly 8-10% either way (margin within 25bp, the bear case 10% below consensus). Against that, the price has a sudden-move history on cash prints ((20)% in March 2026), a 2.4x lease-inclusive net debt with 70% floating, unhedged 30% non-euro revenue, a North American customer concentration and a thin float: between Banca Generali (60) and NKT (54).

#10 Lifecycle phase: the thesis is Broadening and the price is a phase behind

Thesis broadening with the price turning up is the combination that pays best if the next two releases confirm, and the March 2027 results decide the next phase.

The dashboard's rule puts the stock in "Broadening", and the Analyst agrees, with one qualification. Broadening is right for the thesis: new geographies (Canada in 2025, Australia in 2026), a new growth engine (North America at 19% of sales and growing 48%), record launches, estimates rising for a sixth month, and all six brokers at Buy. The price is a phase behind: it has been "bottoming to turning up" since the September low (EUR 316.5, 19.5x), is 9% above a 200-day average that has only just turned, and sits at the 42nd percentile of its ten-year multiple range.

The combination pays best on confirmation because the multiple has room to rise before the "Reinforcing" phase is reached. The same combination stalls if the margin leg fails, because the market has already given credit for growth once (26 to 33x in 2024 to 2025) and taken it back.

Held below the top because the margin leg that would confirm broadening into profits is not yet reported and the 2024-25 re-rating was once given and taken back: between AQ Group (78) and Reply (73).

#11 The fair multiple: the guideline is 28.6x, the Analyst's own fair multiple is 25x

At 21.9x the market is paying a below-median multiple for above-median growth, and that gap is the mispricing. The sell-side's EUR 514 median target implies about 29x 2027 earnings. The Analyst uses the guideline 28.6x in #12 as instructed but sets an own fair multiple of 25x; the difference is the 14% of return that depends on the market forgiving the cash profile.

The guideline from the Phases page is 28.6x two-year-forward earnings: the 80th percentile of the ten-year range for a Broadening stock, and 30% above today's 21.9x. In the ten-year distribution the 10th percentile is 16.4x, the median 22.9x, the 75th percentile 27.4x and the 90th 32.1x; the five-year range is 18.0x to 37.8x, with a median of 24.6x. The stock traded at 26 to 33x throughout 2024 and 2025 on 14 to 19% revenue growth and 4.4% margins, so 28.6x is not a stretch relative to history.

Why the Analyst would pay 25 to 26x rather than 28.6x: 28.6x is the right guideline for the phase but the upper end of what the Analyst would pay for this foundation, for four reasons.

  1. Free cash flow to equity after lease cash is thin, and the market has twice (2022 and 2026) punished the stock for it.
  2. The margin is 4.4%, with no demonstrated path above 5%.
  3. The governance and free-float discount is permanent.
  4. The 2024 to 2025 multiples were set in a lower-rate regime, with a narrower French premium.

The Analyst therefore sets 25 to 26x as fair for a Broadening phase at this quality, between the ten-year median and the 75th percentile, and treats 28.6x as the better case, which requires the margin leg to be visible. Against peers, 25x two-year-forward earnings compares with Kuehne + Nagel at 21x on 5% EPS growth and GXO at about 22x on 4 to 5% organic growth; ID Logistics' 20%-plus EPS compounding justifies the premium.

A modest premium to peers buys four times their growth.

#12 Total shareholder return: about +34% in the base case and a probability-weighted +27% over 18 months

The base-case return is about +34% over 18 months, rising to +50 to +57% at the guideline multiple, against a plausible (20)% if the margin leg fails; the probability-weighted return of +27% confirms the positive skew.

The starting point: at a price of EUR 383.5, two-year-forward EPS on the Analyst's numbers is about EUR 17.9 (11/12 of FY2028 and 1/12 of FY2027), a P/E of 21.4x. On consensus, two-year-forward EPS is EUR 17.67, a P/E of 21.7x.

Over 6 to 18 months (to end-2027 or mid-2028): two-year-forward EPS rolls to about EUR 20.1 (FY2029) at end-2027 and about EUR 21.0 (a blend of FY2029 and FY2030) at mid-2028, an EPS contribution of +12% to +17%. The multiple moving from 21.4x to the guideline 28.6x adds +34%, and there is no dividend. The total is 1.12 x 1.34 = +50% at 13 months and 1.17 x 1.34 = +57% at 18 months; at the Analyst's own 25x, the total is +31% and +37%. Buybacks serve only the liquidity contract and add nothing.

Over three years (to end-2029): two-year-forward EPS reaches about EUR 24.3 (FY2031, taken as FY2030 plus 9%), +36%. With the multiple at 28.6x (+34%), the total is +82%, about 22% a year; at 25x it is +59%, about 17% a year; at the ten-year median of 22.9x it is +45%, about 13% a year, almost all of it from earnings.

Even at the ten-year median multiple the return is positive at every horizon; the guideline adds about 30 points on top.
